_comment: Hip-core corridor — hip bursitis, gluteal tendinopathy, and post-hip-replacement strengthening; builds around glute-bridge, single-leg-bridge, and clamshell already seeded in the knee corridor. Authored in-house (original instruction text; exercise mechanics are facts, phrasing is ours).

exercises.name: Isometric Hip Abduction (Wall Press)
instructions: Stand tall side-on to a wall with your working leg closest to it, fingertips resting on the wall for balance.
Keep the working leg straight with toes facing forward, and press the outer edge of that foot firmly into the base of the wall.
Build the push up gradually to a strong but comfortable effort — nothing moves, the outer hip simply switches on. Ease off if pain sharpens.
Hold the press while breathing normally, then release just as gradually.

exercises.name: Side-Lying Hip Abduction
instructions: Lie on your side with the working leg on top, body in one straight line, bottom knee softly bent for stability.
Point the top leg's toes slightly toward the floor and keep the leg in line with your trunk — drifting it forward hands the work to the wrong muscles.
Lift the top leg toward the ceiling about 45 degrees, moving from the hip while the pelvis stays stacked and still.
Lower slowly with control. If your waist hikes or the pelvis rolls back, shrink the range.

exercises.name: Standing Hip Abduction
instructions: Stand tall beside a counter or chair back, resting one hand on it for balance.
Shift your weight fully onto the supporting leg without leaning your trunk toward it.
Sweep the working leg straight out to the side, toes facing forward, keeping your body upright.
Pause, then bring the leg back with control — leaning the trunk is the most common cheat, and the standing hip is working just as hard.

exercises.name: Fire Hydrant
instructions: Start on hands and knees with hands under shoulders, knees under hips, and back flat.
Keeping the knee bent, lift one knee out to the side — like a dog at a hydrant — only as far as the pelvis stays level.
Move from the hip; the lower back and shoulders stay quiet.
Lower slowly to the start. If the trunk twists, shrink the lift.

exercises.name: Banded Lateral Walk
instructions: Loop a resistance band around both legs just above the knees and stand with feet hip-width apart so the band is lightly taut.
Sink into a shallow athletic stance — hips back, knees soft, chest up.
Step sideways with the lead foot, then follow part-way with the trailing foot so the band never goes slack.
Keep the knees tracking over the toes and stay at one height — no bobbing up and down.
Lead with the other leg to travel back the same way.

exercises.name: Prone Hip Extension
instructions: Lie face down with both legs straight and your forehead resting on your hands.
Gently draw in the lower belly, then squeeze the buttock of the working side before anything moves.
Keeping the knee straight, lift that leg a few inches off the floor — the lift comes from the buttock, not the lower back.
Pause at the top, then lower slowly. If the low back arches or pinches, lift lower.

exercises.name: Standing Hip Extension
instructions: Stand tall facing a counter or chair back, both hands resting on it.
Squeeze the buttock first, then sweep the working leg straight behind you with the knee straight.
Move only from the hip — stop the sweep before the lower back arches or the trunk tips forward.
Return with control and stand tall between repetitions.

exercises.name: Figure-4 Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat.
Cross the ankle of the stretch-side leg over the opposite thigh and let that knee fall comfortably outward — the legs form a figure 4.
Reach through the gap, clasp behind the supporting thigh, and draw it gently toward your chest until you feel a stretch deep in the buttock.
Keep your head and shoulders heavy on the floor, breathe slowly, and hold — a stretch, never a sharp pinch.
If you have had a hip replacement, check with your therapist before adding this position.

exercises.name: Standing Hip-Flexor Stretch
instructions: Stand in a split stance with the stretch-side foot well behind you, holding a chair back if you need balance.
Tuck your tailbone under and squeeze the rear-side buttock — the front of that hip should already begin to lengthen.
Keeping the trunk upright, shift your weight gently forward onto the front leg until you feel a stretch across the front of the rear hip.
Hold there and breathe — if the lower back arches, the stretch has moved to the wrong place; re-tuck and ease off.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Stance
instructions: Stand tall beside a counter or chair back with fingertips resting lightly on it.
Shift your weight onto one leg and lift the other foot just clear of the floor.
Keep the pelvis level and the standing knee soft — no sagging into the outer hip.
As you steady, hover the fingertips just off the support; progress later by standing on a balance pad.

exercises.name: Standing March with Band
instructions: Loop a small resistance band around both feet and stand tall, a counter or chair back within reach.
March one knee up toward hip height against the band, keeping the trunk tall — no leaning back.
Keep the standing-side pelvis steady; it should not dip or sway as the knee rises.
Lower that foot with control and march the other side, alternating in a slow, deliberate rhythm.

exercises.name: Pelvic Drop
instructions: Stand sideways on a low step on your working leg, the other foot hanging free off the edge — steady yourself on a wall or rail if needed.
Keeping both knees straight, let the free-side pelvis drop slowly so that foot lowers toward the floor — stop if pain sharpens over the standing-side outer hip.
Push through the standing hip to hike the pelvis level again, lifting the free foot back up.
All the movement comes from the pelvis — the standing-leg outer hip does the work, and the slow drop matters as much as the lift.

progressions.note: Move from holds to lifting repetitions once a long, firm wall press causes no flare-up by the next morning.
Progress upright when you can lift through the full range with the pelvis stacked and no next-day outer-hip soreness.
Add band resistance once the standing sweep stays smooth on both sides with the trunk tall and the hand only hovering.
Progress to upright banded work when the pelvis stays level through the full lift on both sides.
Move upright once the straight leg clears the floor without the lower back arching.
Add the marching band once you can balance hands-free for the full prescribed time with a level pelvis.
Progress to step work when hands-free stance is steady and the pelvis holds level for the whole time.
Progress when full-width walks keep constant band tension and the knees track over the toes without wobble.
